deck.name: Git Concepts and Commands
deck.description: How Git stores history, what the staging area is for, how branches, merges and rebases really work, how to undo almost anything, and which commands you need for day-to-day work. Written for people who use Git already but want the model behind the commands. Behaviour described here is stable across modern Git releases; where a feature arrived in a specific version it says so.

topics.description: The four object types and how history is shaped.
The index, the three trees, and comparing them.
Refs, HEAD, fast-forward and merge commits.
Reset, revert, reflog and getting work back.
Fetch, pull, push, tracking branches and force-push safety.
Log, diff, blame, bisect and grep.
Config levels, ignore rules, attributes and hooks.

notes.front: Which four object types does Git store?
notes.back: Blobs, trees, commits and annotated tags.

notes.front: What does a blob object hold?
notes.back: The contents of one file, with no name and no history attached.

notes.front: What does a tree object hold?
notes.back: A list of names, each pointing at a blob or another tree, which is how a directory is represented.

notes.front: What does a commit object record?
notes.back: A pointer to one tree, pointers to its parent commits, and the author, committer and message.

notes.front: How is an object's name produced?
notes.back: By hashing the object's type, size and contents.

notes.front: Which hash algorithm do Git repositories use by default, and what is the alternative?
notes.back: SHA-1 by default, with SHA-256 repositories available as an experimental option.

notes.front: How long is a SHA-1 object name in hexadecimal characters?
notes.back: 40 characters

notes.front: What happens to every commit hash when you change an old commit's content?
notes.back: That commit and every commit built on top of it get new hashes, because a commit names its parents.

notes.front: Does Git store history as a series of changes or as a series of snapshots?
notes.back: As snapshots of the whole tree, with differences worked out later when you ask for them.

notes.front: What shape does Git's commit history have?
notes.back: A directed acyclic graph, since each commit points back at its parents.

notes.front: How many parents does a merge commit have?
notes.back: Two or more, one for each line of history being joined.

notes.front: How many parents does a root commit have?
notes.back: None, which is what makes it the start of the history.

notes.front: Which extra information does an annotated tag object store, compared with a lightweight tag?
notes.back: A tagger, a date and a message, stored as an object of its own.

notes.front: What is a lightweight tag actually stored as?
notes.back: A ref pointing straight at a commit, with no tag object involved.

notes.front: What are packfiles for?
notes.back: Storing many objects in one compressed file, with similar objects reduced to deltas, which keeps repositories small.

notes.front: Which command reports how many loose objects and packs a repository holds?
notes.back: git count-objects -v

notes.text: A {{c1::blob}} holds file contents, a {{c2::tree}} holds names pointing at blobs and subtrees, and a {{c3::commit}} holds a tree plus its parents.
notes.extra: None of the three stores a filename with the content itself.

notes.text: Because an object is named after a hash of its contents, editing a file produces a {{c1::new}} object rather than changing the old one.
notes.extra: That is what makes history tamper-evident.

notes.front: What is the staging area also called?
notes.back: The index, and it is stored in a single file inside the Git directory.

notes.front: What is the staging area for?
notes.back: Deciding exactly which changes go into the next commit, which allows a partial commit.

notes.front: Which three trees does Git compare when reporting status?
notes.back: HEAD, the index and the working tree.

notes.front: What does git diff show with no arguments?
notes.back: Changes in the working tree that are not staged yet.

notes.front: What does git diff --staged show?
notes.back: The changes staged in the index, compared against the last commit.

notes.front: What does git diff HEAD compare?
notes.back: The working tree against the last commit, so staged and unstaged changes both appear.

notes.front: Which command stages parts of a file rather than the whole file?
notes.back: git add -p, which walks through the changes a hunk at a time.

notes.front: What does git commit -a stage for you?
notes.back: Modifications and deletions of files that are already tracked, while leaving new files alone.

notes.front: Which command takes a file out of the index while keeping it on disk?
notes.back: git rm --cached, which is the way to stop tracking a file you want to keep.

notes.front: What does git restore do in modern Git?
notes.back: Restores file contents in the working tree, from the index by default.

notes.front: How do you unstage a file without losing its changes?
notes.back: git restore --staged, which copies the version from HEAD back into the index.

notes.front: Which older command does git restore replace?
notes.back: git checkout -- for file paths, which arrived in Git 2.23 alongside git switch.

notes.front: What are the two common prefixes in short status output?
notes.back: Two question marks for an untracked file, and a letter such as M or A for a tracked file that changed or was added.

notes.front: What does git status --short show that the long form also shows?
notes.back: The staged state in the left column and the unstaged state in the right column.

notes.front: What does git stash do by default?
notes.back: Saves tracked modifications and the index, then returns the working tree to the last commit.

notes.front: Which flag makes git stash include untracked files?
notes.back: -u

notes.front: What is the difference between git stash pop and git stash apply?
notes.back: pop also drops the stash entry after applying it, while apply leaves it in the list.

notes.front: Which command shows the contents of a stash as a diff?
notes.back: git stash show -p

notes.front: What does git clean -fd remove?
notes.back: Untracked files and directories, which is why a dry run with -n comes first.

notes.text: The staging area is the {{c1::index}}, and git diff --staged compares it against {{c2::HEAD}}.
notes.extra: Plain git diff instead compares the working tree against the index.

notes.front: What is a Git branch, technically?
notes.back: A movable pointer to one commit, stored as a ref under refs/heads.

notes.front: What does HEAD point at?
notes.back: The branch you are on, by holding a symbolic ref to it.

notes.front: What does it mean when HEAD points straight at a commit?
notes.back: You are in detached HEAD state, and new commits belong to no branch until you name one.

notes.front: How do you keep commits you made in detached HEAD state?
notes.back: Point a new branch at the current commit with git branch or git switch -c.

notes.front: Which command creates a branch and moves to it?
notes.back: git switch -c, or git checkout -b in older releases.

notes.front: What does git switch - do?
notes.back: Returns to the branch you were on before the current one.

notes.front: What is a fast-forward merge?
notes.back: Moving the branch pointer forward when the other branch is already an ancestor, which needs no merge commit.

notes.front: Which flag forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible?
notes.back: --no-ff, which keeps a record that a branch existed.

notes.front: What does a three-way merge use to combine two branches?
notes.back: The merge base, meaning the most recent commit both branches share.

notes.front: Which three marker lines appear in a file with a merge conflict?
notes.back: A line of angle brackets with HEAD, a line of equals signs, and a line of angle brackets with the other branch name.

notes.front: Which command abandons a merge in progress?
notes.back: git merge --abort

notes.front: What does git merge --squash produce?
notes.back: Staged changes from the branch, leaving you to write one commit yourself instead of a merge commit.

notes.front: What is an octopus merge?
notes.back: A merge of more than two branches at once, which produces one commit with several parents.

notes.front: Which command deletes a branch that has already been merged?
notes.back: git branch -d, and -D forces the deletion of an unmerged branch.

notes.front: Which command renames the current branch?
notes.back: git branch -m

notes.front: What does git branch -vv add to the branch list?
notes.back: Each branch's upstream branch and how far ahead or behind it is.

notes.front: Which command lists the branches that contain a given commit?
notes.back: git branch --contains

notes.front: What does HEAD^ mean?
notes.back: The first parent of the current commit, while HEAD^2 names the second parent of a merge.

notes.front: What does HEAD~3 mean?
notes.back: Three commits back along the first-parent line.

notes.front: Which worktree files does git switch touch when moving between branches?
notes.back: Those that differ between the branches, so uncommitted changes can block the move.

notes.text: A fast-forward merge only moves the {{c1::branch pointer}}, so it creates no {{c2::merge commit}}.
notes.extra: Use --no-ff when you want the merge recorded as its own commit.

notes.front: What does git rebase do to your commits?
notes.back: Replays them on top of another commit, producing new commits with new hashes.

notes.front: Why is rebasing a branch that others already have a bad idea?
notes.back: The rewritten commits have new hashes, so everyone else's history diverges from yours.

notes.front: Which commands does interactive rebase offer for each commit?
notes.back: Pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup and drop.

notes.front: What is the practical difference between squash and fixup in an interactive rebase?
notes.back: Squash lets you edit the combined message, while fixup keeps the earlier message and discards the later one.

notes.front: What does git rebase --autosquash do?
notes.back: Moves commits created with --fixup or --squash next to their target and marks them for squashing.

notes.front: What does git commit --amend change?
notes.back: Replaces the most recent commit with a new one containing the staged changes.

notes.front: What does git rebase --onto let you do?
notes.back: Move a range of commits onto a different base, which is useful for lifting a branch off the wrong parent.

notes.front: What does git cherry-pick create?
notes.back: A new commit on the current branch containing the change from one commit elsewhere.

notes.front: Does cherry-picking preserve the original commit hash?
notes.back: No, the copy has a new hash because it has a different parent.

notes.front: What does git filter-repo or filter-branch exist to do?
notes.back: Rewrite a whole history, for example to remove a file that should never have been committed.

notes.front: What does git rerere save you from doing twice?
notes.back: Resolving the same merge conflict again, by recording how you resolved it the first time.

notes.text: Interactive rebase is the usual way to {{c1::squash}} several small commits into one before sharing them.
notes.extra: Once pushed and shared, rewriting needs care and coordination.

notes.front: What does git reset --soft do?
notes.back: Moves the branch pointer while leaving the index and working tree untouched, so changes look staged.

notes.front: What does git reset --mixed do, and is it the default?
notes.back: Moves the branch pointer and clears the index, leaving the working tree alone, and this is the default mode.

notes.front: What does git reset --hard discard?
notes.back: Both the staged and the unstaged changes in tracked files, which makes it the dangerous mode.

notes.front: How does git revert differ from git reset?
notes.back: Revert adds a new commit that undoes an earlier one, so it is safe on shared history.

notes.front: What does the -m flag mean for git revert?
notes.back: It names which parent of a merge commit counts as the mainline to undo against.

notes.front: What does the reflog record?
notes.back: Where HEAD and each branch tip have pointed locally, and when.

notes.front: How do you recover a commit that a hard reset discarded?
notes.back: Find it in git reflog and reset or branch to that entry.

notes.front: Why is the reflog not a backup of your repository?
notes.back: Entries are local, expire after a while, and vanish when old objects are pruned.

notes.front: Which two reflog expiry periods do the defaults set?
notes.back: Reachable entries last 90 days and unreachable ones 30 days.

notes.front: What does git fsck report?
notes.back: Objects that are missing or corrupt, and commits or blobs that nothing points at.

notes.front: Which flag asks git fsck to save unreachable objects for inspection?
notes.back: --lost-found

notes.front: What does git gc collect?
notes.back: Loose objects into packs and unreachable objects into the bin, which keeps a repository tidy.

notes.front: What makes a deleted file recoverable if you committed it at some point?
notes.back: The blob still exists until pruning, so any commit that referenced it can be reached again.

notes.text: git reset --soft moves the branch pointer only, --mixed also clears the {{c1::index}}, and --hard also rewrites the {{c2::working tree}}.
notes.extra: Only the last of the three throws work away.

notes.text: A local safety net records every movement of HEAD, and it is called the {{c1::reflog}}.
notes.extra: It lives only on your machine and expires.

notes.text: To undo a commit that other people already have, use {{c1::git revert}}, which adds a {{c2::new commit}} rather than rewriting history.
notes.extra: Rewriting shared history forces everyone else to recover.

notes.front: What does git fetch change in your working tree?
notes.back: Nothing, since it only downloads objects and updates remote-tracking refs.

notes.front: Which two steps does git pull perform?
notes.back: A fetch followed by a merge or a rebase, depending on your configuration.

notes.front: Which command makes pull rebase instead of merging?
notes.back: git pull --rebase, or the pull.rebase configuration setting.

notes.front: What is a remote-tracking branch such as origin/main?
notes.back: Your local record of where that branch was on the remote when you last fetched.

notes.front: What does the -u flag on git push do?
notes.back: Sets the upstream branch, so later pushes and pulls need no arguments.

notes.front: Why does git push normally refuse a non-fast-forward update?
notes.back: It would discard commits on the remote that you have not taken into account.

notes.front: Why is --force-with-lease safer than --force?
notes.back: It refuses the push if the remote moved since your last fetch, so you cannot silently erase someone's work.

notes.front: Which command deletes a branch on the remote?
notes.back: git push origin --delete, naming the branch.

notes.front: Which flag makes git fetch remove remote-tracking branches that no longer exist on the remote?
notes.back: --prune

notes.front: Which flag sends annotated tags along with the commits being pushed?
notes.back: --follow-tags

notes.front: Does git push send tags by default?
notes.back: No, tags need an explicit push, unlike branches.

notes.front: What does git clone --depth 1 produce?
notes.back: A shallow clone with only the most recent commit and no earlier history.

notes.front: Which option makes a partial clone that skips file contents until they are needed?
notes.back: --filter=blob:none

notes.front: Which command shows the URLs a repository's remotes point at?
notes.back: git remote -v

notes.front: What is a submodule?
notes.back: A pointer to one commit of another repository, recorded inside the parent repository.

notes.front: What does git worktree add give you?
notes.back: A second working directory attached to the same repository, so two branches can be checked out at once.

notes.front: Which commits does git log main..feature list?
notes.back: Those reachable from feature but absent from main, which is what you are about to push.

notes.text: git fetch downloads objects and updates {{c1::remote-tracking}} refs, while git pull goes on to {{c2::merge}} or rebase.
notes.extra: Fetch first when you want to look before you leap.

notes.front: Which git log flag draws the commit graph as text?
notes.back: --graph

notes.front: Which git log flag shows one line per commit?
notes.back: --oneline

notes.front: Which git log flag follows a file through renames?
notes.back: --follow, given a single path.

notes.front: What does git log -S search for?
notes.back: Commits that changed the number of occurrences of a string, which finds when code appeared or vanished.

notes.front: What does git blame show for each line of a file?
notes.back: The last commit that changed that line, with its author and date.

notes.front: Which flag tells git blame to ignore whitespace-only changes?
notes.back: -w

notes.front: What is git bisect doing between a good and a bad commit?
notes.back: A binary search, checking out a midpoint for you to test at each step.

notes.front: What does git bisect run automate?
notes.back: The whole search, by running a command at each step and reading its exit status.

notes.front: Which command prints the type of an object, such as commit or blob?
notes.back: git cat-file -t

notes.front: Which command shows a commit's message and its changes together?
notes.back: git show

notes.front: What does git grep search?
notes.back: The files tracked by the repository, which makes it fast and predictable.

notes.front: What does git shortlog -sn produce?
notes.back: A list of authors with their commit counts, most prolific first.

notes.front: Which command counts the commits reachable from a ref?
notes.back: git rev-list --count

notes.front: Which command names a commit in terms of the nearest tag?
notes.back: git describe

notes.front: What does git diff --stat give you instead of a patch?
notes.back: A per-file summary of how many lines changed.

notes.front: Which command writes a set of commits as files you can email?
notes.back: git format-patch

notes.text: When a bug appeared somewhere in a long history, {{c1::git bisect}} finds the offending commit in roughly {{c2::logarithmic}} time.
notes.extra: For 1000 commits that is about ten tests.

notes.front: Which three levels can Git configuration live at?
notes.back: System, global for your user, and local to the repository.

notes.front: Which configuration level wins when settings conflict?
notes.back: The most specific one, so local beats global and global beats system.

notes.front: Which flag shows the file each configuration value came from?
notes.back: --show-origin, useful with git config --list.

notes.front: What are the two settings a commit needs from your configuration?
notes.back: user.name and user.email.

notes.front: Which configuration setting chooses the name for new branches?
notes.back: init.defaultBranch

notes.front: Where does Git look for a repository's ignore rules?
notes.back: The .gitignore file in the working tree, plus a private file in the Git directory.

notes.front: What does a trailing slash in a gitignore pattern mean?
notes.back: The pattern matches a directory rather than a file of that name.

notes.front: What does a leading exclamation mark do in a gitignore file?
notes.back: Re-includes a path that an earlier pattern excluded.

notes.front: Which pattern in a gitignore file matches every directory with a given name at any depth?
notes.back: The bare name without a leading slash, such as build.

notes.front: Which command explains why a file is being ignored, and by which rule?
notes.back: git check-ignore -v

notes.front: Does adding a file to gitignore stop Git from tracking it if it is already tracked?
notes.back: No, because ignore rules only apply to untracked files.

notes.front: What is .gitattributes used for?
notes.back: Per-path settings such as line-ending handling, diff drivers and export rules.

notes.front: What does the core.autocrlf setting control?
notes.back: Whether Git converts line endings between the index and the working tree on different platforms.

notes.front: Where do repository hooks live?
notes.back: In the hooks directory inside the Git directory, which is why they are not cloned.

notes.front: Which hook runs before a commit message is finalised?
notes.back: commit-msg

notes.front: Which hook runs before a commit is created and can reject it?
notes.back: pre-commit

notes.front: Which configuration setting points Git at a shared hooks directory?
notes.back: core.hooksPath

notes.text: Ignore rules apply only to {{c1::untracked}} files, so a file that is already tracked needs {{c2::git rm --cached}} before the rule takes effect.
notes.extra: That keeps the file on disk while removing it from the index.

notes.text: Git configuration is read from the system, {{c1::global}} and local levels, and the most {{c2::specific}} value wins.
notes.extra: git config --list --show-origin reveals where each value came from.
